title: Statement on AI
text:
In the age where AI is increasingly involved not only in an academic setting, but also in our daily lives, it is both important and necessary to create and follow a personal policy regarding one’s AI use.
There are generally four outcomes when we are faced with a problem in which we might consider using AI to solve (Cipolli 2026). We can decide against using AI at all, verify its suggestions with our own background knowledge, blindly follow it towards a correct answer, or blindly follow it towards an incorrect answer. I believe that relying on AI for answers where we don’t completely understand its sources, methods, or concepts will lead to a society in which humans will lose their autonomy in the workforce, and eventually in their own lives. If we don’t do our own thinking, then our functions in the workplace and in academics will become obsolete.
However, using AI to help us overcome barriers, unexpected issues, or to explain certain concepts that help us along the way of solving a problem can be super beneficial. Rather than spending hours trying to fix a bug that human error may miss, AI can quickly scan an entire file and notice one wrong button that was pressed. Using AI to make our lives more efficient to pave the way for learning, rather than doing the learning for us, is a great way to become an ethical statistical practitioner, as mentioned in the Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice (American Statistical Association 2022).
Not only does unethical AI use harm us, it also indirectly harms the people who might rely on our work. Passing work done by AI as your own is both an issue of plaigiarism and responsibility, and others might trust and cite your work as authentic and true, when in reality they are now citing AI (American Statistical Association 2022). It is important that we stay honest with the people we collaborate with and disclose all AI use, with plans to remedy any instances of unethical AI use.




References

American Statistical Association. 2022. Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice. Committee on Professional Ethics.


Cipolli, William. 2026. AI Statement.

Compute the maximum likelihood estimates using optim() in R as described in lecture 16: \[\max_{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\}).\]



Code
# Negative log-likelihood where theta = c(beta0, beta1, sigma)
neg.llike <- function(theta, x, y) {
  b0 <-    theta[1]
  b1 <-    theta[2]
  sigma <- theta[3]
  mu <- b0 + b1 * x                # E(Y | x)
  -sum(dnorm(y, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

mle <- optim(par = c(mean(y), 0, sd(y)),   # starting values
             fn  = neg.llike,
             x = x, y = y,

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
1.1 Part a
Complete the following steps in \(R=1000\) simulations.

Simulate data for \(k=5\) samples \(n=30\) drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution.
Use pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method="none") to compute unadjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.
Use rstatix::tukey_hsd(...) to compute the Tukey’s HSD adjusted pairwise tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.

In the end, describe the Type I error rates.



Code
set.seed(1212)

k <- 5    # number of samples
n <- 30   # sample size
R <- 1000 # simulations

group <- factor(rep(1:k, each = n))

sig_none <- logical(R)
sig_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {

  value <- rnorm(k * n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  sim_data <- tibble(group = group, value = value)

  sig_none[i] <- any(pairwise.t.test(x = sim_data$value,
                                      g = sim_data$group,
                                      p.adjust.method = "none")$p.value < 0.05,
                      na.rm = TRUE)

  sig_tukey[i] <- any(tukey_hsd(aov(value ~ group, data = sim_data))$p.adj < 0.05)

}

# Type 1 error rates
mean(sig_none)


[1] 0.279


Code
mean(sig_tukey)


[1] 0.049



The Type 1 error rate for the uncorrected test is 27.9%, while the Type 1 error rate for the corrected test is 4.9%, which is close to 5%. This makes sense because the corrected test caps the FWER at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The uncorrected test has a much higher chance of detecting a difference when there is none (detecting noise) than the corrected test.

text:
A benefit of using the Wilcox signed rank test is that the researchers don’t have to assume normality for the underlying population distribution, as that is unknown and the sample size is not large enough for the CLT. However, there are a few concerns to using this test:

The data collected are proportions that represent the number of times the GWL dogs correctly retrieved the new toy when requested out of 12 requests. The fact that this data is discrete with only 13 possible unique observations leads to multiple tied observations in the data. Using the exact Wilcoxon distribution could be an issue due to having many ties, and the authors would need to account for them in order to use an accurate Wilcoxon distribution.
Due to n=10, the sample size is likely not large enough to use an asymptotic distribution because n would usually need to be at least 50. Because the authors didn’t specify which distribution they used, this could be an issue.
The boundedness of the range of the data (0, 1), and the fact that 4 dogs had a proportion of 1.000 is a concern for the symmetry assumption for the Wilcoxon signed rank test. We don’t know the underlying distribution, and we definitely don’t have evidence supporting that it might be symmetric from the sample data.

A one-sample t-test is constrained by the assumption that the population is normally distributed and the population variance exists, both of which we don’t know, and the sample size of n = 10 does not satisfy the CLT. Since the sample data is skewed left, we don’t have evidence that the population distribution is normally distributed from the sample data. Moreover, a one-sample z-test for proportions also does not have a sample size large enough for the CLT. Due to the issues with the sample size, I think the best choice would be to use an exact binomial test because we don’t have to worry about our population data being normally distributed or about the CLT (relies on the binomial distribution). We can frame the data to be Bernoulli by interpreting each dog as a success if it retrieved the new toy correctly more than 50% of the time.



We are aiming to evaluate whether GWL dogs can correctly retrieve a new toy when requested better than chance (50%), aftering overhearing two people reference the object while not addressing the dog. n = 10 dogs were requested 12 times to retrieve the new toy, and our data present the proportion of times the dog correctly retrieved it.
Our null hypothesis is that H0: p = 0.50 and Ha: p > 0.50 and conducting a one-sided exact binomial test using alpha = 0.05, where a success means that the dog retrieved the new toy correctly more than half the time. We decided to use the exact binomial test because we violate no assumptions; our data does not satisfy the normality/CLT condition for a one-sample t-test, does not satisfy the symmetric assumption for a Wilcox signed rank test, and does not satisfy the sample size / CLT condition for a one-sample z-test for proportions.

                          n = n,                    # sample size (trials)

title: Homework 4 – Regression Consult
text:
When people make decisions, their choices are often swayed by how information is presented. This is often described as “the framing effect.” One example of this, is how commercials describe new medications. As an example, Nereus (tradipitant), a new drug for motion-induced vomiting like sea-sickness, is marketed with a positive frame as reducing vomiting incidence from 44% to 18% (a reduction of 60%). This marketing makes it seem more effective than a negative frame that says just 18% of patients still experienced vomiting, even though both statements are true.
Xu (2024) aimed to evaluate whether older adults are more or less vulnerable to framing than younger adults. They collected a sample of 696 adults aged 18 to 71 and exposed them to three different scenarios
Scenario 1: Rate Drug Efficacy (1 = very bad, 6 = very good)
Scenario 2: Likelihood to stop drinking cocoa (1 = surely stop, 6 = surely continue)
Scenario 3: Preference for chance choice (1 = surely safe option, 6 = surely risky)
In each scenario, participants were randomly assigned a positive or negative frame. They rated their response on a 1-6 scale. The researchers want to build three models, one for each scenario adjusting for simultaneous linear changes in demographic variables (gender, ethnicity, education level, political affiliation).
They want to evaluate whether, as adults age, the way choices are worded have more influence on their judgments and ultimate choices. If there is a change, are those changes driven by positive or negative framings? At what age does this effect onset?

title: Homework 4 – Regression Consult
text:
4.1 Discussion
Across all three scenarios, the framing effect shows that the gap between the positive and negative frames widens with age. The widening comes almost entirely from the negative frame. In every scenario, the positive-frame age slope was essentially zero. Under the negative frame, older adults rated the drug as less effective, were more likely to say they would stop drinking cocoa, and preferred the risky program more. The strength of the evidence differs by scenario. The frame × age interaction was statistically discernible only for risky-choice framing. For attribute and goal framing, it was in the predicted direction but not discernible at \(\alpha = 0.05\). All three interactions had very small effect sizes. On the question of onset, the framing effect in the attribute scenario was present at every age from 18 to 71, so it has no onset age. For goal and risky-choice framing, the Johnson-Neyman analysis showed that the framing effect was not discernible among the youngest adults and became discernible around 26 or 27, persisting through to 71 (the oldest age).
These findings matter because older adults increasingly make high-stakes health and financial decisions, and much of the information they receive is framed in terms of losses. Our results suggest that loss-framed messages, rather than gain-framed ones, are the ones whose influence grows with age. Communicators such as clinicians, pharmaceutical advertisers, and advertising campaigns could therefore shift older adults’ judgments more by choosing negative wording, even when the information and outcome is the same.
Our conclusions are more cautious than Xu (2024), and the differences come from several changes to the analysis:

Data cleaning: The paper reported excluding participants who failed the attention check or gave mismatched ages, yet its N = 696 equals every completed survey in the data. We applied those exclusions, removing 8 participants, and treated “Prefer not to say” as missing rather than as a demographic group.
Model conditions: The paper reported no checks of model conditions. We assessed residuals, influence, and multicollinearity for each model and found non-Gaussian, unequal-variance errors caused by the bounded 1–6 scale, which we addressed with a Box-Cox transformation.
Frame-specific slopes: The paper estimated these by fitting separate regressions to each frame’s subset without the demographic controls. We estimated them with emtrends() from the full adjusted model.
Interpreting the interaction: The paper treated interactions with p = .087 and .111 as evidence that age moderates framing in every scenario. Our results support that claim only for risky-choice framing.

This study has several limitations. The participants were an MTurk convenience sample and were mostly White, college-educated, and Democrat, so the results may not generalize to all U.S. adults. The age distribution of the participants skewed younger, with less being closer to 71 and more being closer to the 20s. Few participants were over 60, and none were over 71.

title: Homework 5 – Regression
text:
1.1 Overview & Analytical Strategy
To evaluate whether framing effects strengthen as adults age—and to identify whether age-related divergence is driven by positive or negative wording—we fit three multiple linear regression models (one per scenario):
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Age}_i + \beta_2 \text{Frame}_i + \beta_3 (\text{Age}_i \times \text{Frame}_i) + \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \epsilon_i\] 
where \(\mathbf{X}_i\) adjusts for simultaneous linear differences across gender, ethnicity, education level, and political affiliation.
 

Interaction (\(\beta_3\)): Tests whether the gap between Positive and Negative framing widens with age. 
Simple Slopes: Evaluates the age slope separately within the Positive frame and the Negative frame to determine which framing drives the change.

I don’t like the explanation of the slopes for age and frame. It should’ve specified specifically that \(\beta_1\) was the effect on perception for a one unit increase in age and that \(\beta_2\) was the effect on perception for a change from negative framing to positive framing. Additionally, it doesn’t specify whether they are using Positive or Negative framing as the baseline. 

Johnson-Neyman (J-N) Analysis: Identifies the exact age threshold (“onset”) at which the conditional difference between Positive and Negative frames becomes statistically significant (\(p < .05\)).

Does framing influence grow with age? Yes—the framing gap widens with age in all three scenarios, reaching statistical significance in Scenario 3 (Chance Choice) (\(p = 0.032\)) and showing a marginal trend in the same direction in Scenario 1 (\(p = 0.087\)) and Scenario 2 (\(p = 0.111\)).
Positive vs. Negative driver: Across every scenario, changes are driven entirely by the negative framing. Ratings in the positive frame remain flat across age (\(p > 0.50\) in all three models), whereas older adults respond significantly more strongly to negative framings (becoming more likely to stop drinking cocoa when warned of increased cancer risk, \(p = 0.022\), and more risk-seeking when outcomes are framed as lives lost, \(p = 0.007\)).
Age of onset: In Scenario 1, the framing effect is already significant at the youngest observed age (\(18\)). In Scenarios 2 and 3, younger adults (ages \(18\text{–}25\)) show no statistically significant framing bias, with the framing effect emerging at age 25.9 (Scenario 2) and age 26.9 (Scenario 3).

I like that the table presents the results that directly answer the research question, and the results discussion addresses the different things being tested, including if framing effect changes with age, whether positive or negative framing had a larger effect, and at around which age the framing effect becomes statistically discernible.

The effect size for the results is missing, which could say a lot about the practical importance of these regression models. Some of the results are overstated through Gemini. It seems like it is trying to say that all three scenarios have discernibly different framing effects with age, but only one of the p-values is significant. Moreover, only two scenarios show that older participants respond more strongly to negative framing, so I wouldn’t say changes are entirely driven by negative framing. Lastly, I’m unsure where Gemini got the age onsets for each scenario, because the Johnson Neyman analysis was testing for the wrong thing.

title: Homework 5 – Regression
text:
3.2 Part b
To see the multicollinearity penalty directly, hold every parameter of a multiple regression model constant except the correlation between predictors.
Suppose we aim to model \[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \epsilon\] where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), \(\beta_1 = 0.25\) is the target effect, \(\beta_2 = 0.30\), and \(X_1, X_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) with \(\text{Cor}(X_1, X_2) = \rho\). In this setting, \(R_1^2 = \rho^2\) and \(\text{VIF}_1 = \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2}\).
Write \(f^2\) out in terms of \(VIF\). What happens to \(f^2\) as we alter the \(VIF\) through \(\rho\)?
With \(\sigma = 1\), \(\sigma^2_{X_1} = 1\), and \(R^2_1 = \rho^2\),
\[
f^2 = \frac{\beta_1^2\, \sigma^2_{X_1}(1 - R_1^2)}{\sigma^2} = \beta_1^2(1 - \rho^2) = \frac{\beta_1^2}{\text{VIF}_1} = \frac{0.0625}{\text{VIF}_1}.
\] As \(|\rho|\) increases, the VIF increases and \(f^2\) decreases. For example, doubling the VIF cuts the effect size in half.
Conduct a power analysis to determine the required sample size \(n\) to achieve \(80\%\) power for inference on \(\beta_1\) for \(\text{VIF}\) values of 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 5.0, and 10. What happens as \(\text{VIF}\) increases?



Code
beta1 <- 0.25
p <- 3 # beta0, beta1, beta2
vif.vals <- c(1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 5.0, 10)

tibble(VIF = vif.vals) |>
  mutate(rho = sqrt(1 - 1/VIF),
         f2  = beta1^2/VIF,
         n   = map_dbl(f2, ~ ceiling(pwr.f2.test(u = 1,
                                                f2 = .x,
                                                sig.level = 0.05,
                                                power = 0.80)$v + p))) |>
  kable(digits = 4)

title: Homework 5 – Regression
text:
3.3 Part c
Now, suppose we’re doing something fun like an interaction model. \[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 (X_1 X_2) + \epsilon\] where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).\) The \(T\) statistic for the test still follows a non-central \(t\)-distribution \[T = \frac{\hat{\beta}_3-0}{\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_3)} \sim t(\beta_\Delta, v=n - \underbrace{p}_{\beta{s}})\] where \[\beta_\Delta = \frac{\beta_3 \, \sigma_{X_1 X_2} \sqrt{1 - R_{X_1 X_2}^2}}{\sigma} \sqrt{n} = \pm f \sqrt{n}\] where \(\sigma^2_{X_1 X_2} = \text{Var}(X_1 X_2)\) and \(R_{X_1 X_2}^2 = R^2\) from the regression: \[(X_1 X_2) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 X_1 + \gamma_2 X_2 + \epsilon.\] This makes \[f^2 = \frac{\beta_3^2 \, \sigma_{X_1 X_2}^2 (1 - R_{X_1 X_2}^2)}{\sigma^2}.\]
Suppose both predictors are binary: \[\begin{align*}
X_{1i} \sim& \text{Bernoulli}(0.50)\\
X_{2i} \sim& \text{Bernoulli}(0.50)\\
\end{align*}\] and \(\beta_0=\beta_1=\beta_2=0\), \(\beta_3=0.50\), and \(\sigma=1\).
As a basis for comparison, conduct a simple power analysis that ignores the interaction (e.g., \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1\)), where \(\beta_1=0.50\).



Code
p <- 2 # beta0, beta1
f2.no.int <- 0.50^2/1^2
(n.simple <- ceiling(pwr.f2.test(u = 1,
                                 f2 = f2.no.int,
                                 sig.level = 0.05,
                                 power = 0.80)$v + p))


[1] 34



Next, conduct a power analysis that ignores the third term is an interaction (e.g., \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_3\)), where \(\beta_3=0.50\).



Code
p <- 4 # beta0, beta1, beta2, beta3
(n.no.int <- ceiling(pwr.f2.test(u = 1,
                                f2 = f2.no.int,
                                sig.level = 0.05,
                                power = 0.80)$v + p))


[1] 36



Assess whether what we did in the previous step worked. Conduct a simulation for the proposed interaction model where \(\beta_3=0.50\). At each iteration, generate data of the size recommended in part (c) and test the interaction coefficient. What is the empirical power?



Code
set.seed(1313)
R <- 1000
int.p <- rep(NA, R)
for(i in 1:R){
  x1 <- rbinom(n = n.no.int, size = 1, prob = 0.50)
  x2 <- rbinom(n = n.no.int, size = 1, prob = 0.50)
  y  <- 0 + 0*x1 + 0*x2 + 0.50*(x1*x2) + rnorm(n = n.no.int, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  int.p[i] <- summary(lm(y ~ x1*x2))$coefficients["x1:x2", "Pr(>|t|)"]
}
mean(int.p < 0.05) # power


[1] 0.084


 The empirical power is around 8.4%, which is very below the recommended 80%.

text:
3.4 Part d
Compute the variance of the product, noting here that \((X_1 X_2) \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.25)\).
\[
\sigma^2_{X_1X_2} = 0.25(1 - 0.25) = 0.1875.
\]



Code
(var.prod <- 0.25*(1 - 0.25))


[1] 0.1875


 The variance of the product is 0.1875.
Create a dataset of \(n=4\) containing all possible combinations of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) with \((X_1X_2)\), then fit the regression model predicting the interaction with the unique terms. Report the \(R^2\).



Code
# create dataset
dat.combos <- tibble(X1 = c(0, 1, 0, 1),
                     X2 = c(0, 0, 1, 1)) |>
  mutate(X1X2 = X1*X2)

# report R2
(R2.prod <- summary(lm(X1X2 ~ X1 + X2, data = dat.combos))$r.squared)


[1] 0.6666667



Next, conduct a power analysis that does not ignore that the third term is an interaction (e.g., \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_3\)), where \(\beta_3=0.50\). You can do this using pwr.f2.test() and specifying the effect size using the anticipated coefficient and the values we just calculated: \[\beta_3^2 \sigma^2_{X_1 X_2}(1 - R^2_{X_1 X_2})\]



Code
# power analysis: not ignoring interacion
p <- 4 # beta0, beta1, beta2, beta3
beta3 <- 0.50
(f2.int <- beta3^2*var.prod*(1 - R2.prod)/1^2)


[1] 0.015625


Code
(n.int <- ceiling(pwr.f2.test(u = 1,
                              f2 = f2.int,
                              sig.level = 0.05,
                              power = 0.80)$v + p))


[1] 507


 The sample size needed to reach a power of 80% is \(n=507\).
How would this change if we specified \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) as being independently drawn from a Bernoulli(\(0.2\)) distribution? A Normal(0,1)?

dat.combos.bern <- tibble(X1 = c(0, 1, 0, 1),
                       X2 = c(0, 0, 1, 1)) |>
  mutate(X1X2 = X1*X2,
         w = dbinom(X1, 1, 0.2)*dbinom(X2, 1, 0.2))
(var.prod.bern <- 0.04*(1 - 0.04))  # X1X2 ~ Bernoulli(0.04)


[1] 0.0384


Code
(R2.prod.bern  <- summary(lm(X1X2 ~ X1 + X2, data = dat.combos.bern, weights = w))$r.squared)


[1] 0.3333333

 We would need a sample size of \(n=1231\) to achieve a power of 80% if \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) were independently drawn from a Bernoulli(\(0.2\)) distribution.

set.seed(1313)
dat.norm <- tibble(X1 = rnorm(1e6), X2 = rnorm(1e6)) |>
